content.text: {"persuasion":"UNPERSUADED","support_scope":"NONE","rationale":"The texts support deathly darkness, mortal peril, affliction, and deliverance into light, but they do not establish a technical boundary between two mountain-kingdoms. The book reaches that result only by combining separate proposed equations—shadow as boundary, mountain as kingdom, and valley as a passage between kingdoms—and then importing them into Psalm 23. The counter-reading directly fits the repeated darkness/light, affliction/deliverance, and danger/comfort contrasts with fewer unsupported steps. The substantial lexical possibility that ṣalmāwet means “deep darkness” rather than a compositional “shadow of death” also directly undermines the entry’s outline-of-Death mechanism.","book_core_identification":"“The Shadow of Death” is the boundary or outline of Death’s mountain-kingdom, crossed by the Shepherd’s people on their passage into Christ’s kingdom.","book_secondary_elaborations":["A shadow is an image, outline, or boundary of its subject.","A valley is the low passage between two mountain-kingdoms.","In Psalm 23 the movement is specifically from Death’s kingdom of darkness into Christ’s kingdom of light and life.","The Shadow of Death is the inverse and opposite of the Shadow of Christ, also called the Shadow of Life."],"unsupported_glossary_assertions":["That Death is represented here as a mountain-kingdom whose boundary is the Shadow of Death.","That every relevant valley is a passage between two symbolic mountain-kingdoms.","That Psalm 23:4 specifically depicts crossing a geopolitical or spiritual border from Death’s kingdom into Christ’s kingdom.","That “Shadow of Life” is an established designation for the Shadow of Christ.","That the Shadow of Christ is the exact inverse or opposite of the Shadow of Death."],"chapter_only_objections":["The chapter’s broader claim that scriptural shadow uniformly means protective shelter is strained by uses describing transience, gloom, or danger.","The chapter’s interpretation of Colossians 2 as protecting continued observance of feasts and sabbaths is not asserted in the glossary entry and is therefore outside this ruling.","The chapter’s universal equation of symbolic mountains with kingdoms extends beyond what Daniel’s interpreted mountain vision establishes in every context."],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"The phrase denotes deep or death-associated darkness: mortal peril, affliction, the proximity or realm of death, and, in Isaiah and the New Testament, spiritual or collective darkness dispelled by divine light. Psalm 23 therefore describes passage through the darkest danger under God’s protection, not a mapped border between two mountain-kingdoms.","counter_core_identification":"Deathly or profound darkness associated with peril, affliction, or the realm and power of death.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"CONTRADICTS","material_core_denial":"The phrase’s referent is darkness and death-associated danger or oppression, not the boundary of a mountain-kingdom ruled by Death.","counter_case":["Psalm 23:4 supplies danger, passage, fear, and divine presence, but mentions neither two mountains nor two kingdoms.","Psalm 107:10,14 places “darkness” and “the shadow of death” in parallel with affliction, imprisonment, and deliverance, naturally describing a condition of gloom and oppression.","Isaiah 9:2 and Luke 1:79 directly contrast darkness and the shadow of death with dawning light, strongly favoring a darkness-to-light image.","Colossians 1:13 supports deliverance from the power of darkness into Christ’s kingdom, but does not identify the Shadow of Death as a territorial boundary or mountain.","First Samuel 17:3 shows only that one particular valley lies between two mountains; it does not define valleys generally as borders between kingdoms.","Daniel 2 identifies its great mountain with God’s kingdom, but does not establish that every mountain is a kingdom or that Death possesses a mountain in Psalm 23.","The supplied lexical alternative, ṣalmût or “deep darkness,” accounts for the relevant usages without treating “shadow” as an outline cast by Death."],"book_explanatory_advantages":["It integrates Psalm 23’s movement “through” the valley with the broader biblical theme of deliverance from darkness into life.","It connects Isaiah 9, Luke 1, Psalm 107, and Colossians 1 into a coherent redemptive movement from darkness to light.","Its kingdom imagery gives theological specificity to Death’s dominion and Christ’s deliverance."],"counter_explanatory_advantages":["It follows the immediate darkness/light and affliction/deliverance contrasts in Psalm 107, Isaiah 9, and Luke 1.","It explains Psalm 23 without importing mountains, kingdoms, or a border not mentioned in the verse.","It accommodates mortal peril, Sheol imagery, spiritual darkness, captivity, and profound gloom as contextual forms of one underlying image.","It remains viable whether the Hebrew is analyzed traditionally as “shadow of death” or lexically as “deep darkness.”"],"evidence_book_core_cannot_explain":["The lexical analysis of ṣalmāwet as a single term meaning “deep darkness” contradicts the entry’s derivation from a shadow understood as Death’s cast outline or boundary.","The repeated direct opposition of the expression to morning or divine light identifies darkness as the operative image; no supplied text identifies it as a boundary between mountain-kingdoms.","Psalm 23 names only a valley and does not provide the two symbolic mountains required by the book’s border model."],"comparative_winner":"COUNTER","decisive_sources":["Psalm 23:4","Psalm 107:10,14","Isaiah 9:2","Luke 1:78-79","Colossians 1:13","The supplied lexical evidence for ṣalmāwet/ṣalmût as “deep darkness”"],"unresolved_objections":["The traditional wording “shadow of death” can retain a genuine association with Death’s power or realm, so the book’s kingdom imagery is a possible theological elaboration even though it is not the best lexical or contextual identification.","The expression “land of the shadow of death” can have quasi-locative force, leaving some room for territorial imagery, though not specifically a mountain-border system."],"confidence":"high"}

support_scope.description: Support for the exact glossary BOOK ENTRY only, never for the supporting chapter as a whole.

book_secondary_elaborations.description: Secondary assertions actually printed in the glossary BOOK ENTRY; exclude chapter-only claims.

unsupported_glossary_assertions.description: Material assertions actually printed in the BOOK ENTRY that the evidence does not support. Must be empty for FULL and nonempty for CORE_ONLY.

chapter_only_objections.description: Objections to applications or arguments found only in the supporting chapter. Preserved for later chapter review and excluded from the glossary scope ruling.
